entry.trigger_summary: Trades 'Stocks in Play' — liquid equities gapping on a fresh catalyst — using a small set of named intraday setups: opening range breakout after letting the first minutes settle, ABCD continuation pattern, VWAP-based trades aligning with institutional flow, and momentum continuation on high-relative-volume names. Each strategy chapter specifies where the technical stop belongs before entry.
entry.notes: Pre-market scanner builds a short watchlist of in-play stocks (gap + news + volume criteria); he advises not initiating in the first ~5 minutes after the open (sources 0, 2, 5).

exit.notes: Stop goes at the technical level that invalidates the setup (below support/VWAP per strategy). Standard management: sell partial at first target, move stop to breakeven, trail remainder to next level. All positions closed intraday (sources 0, 2).

risk_per_trade_pct.note: Hard cap: never risk more than 2% of equity on one trade; if the logical stop implies more, skip the trade. Presented as a maximum, not a typical size.

risk.notes: He mandates a personal daily max-loss circuit breaker as a discipline rule, but no universal number is disclosed (varies by account), so loss_limit stays null (sources 0, 2). Also prescribes minimum 2:1 reward-to-risk before entry.

sizing.notes: Three-step process: fix max dollar risk (<=2% equity), take per-share risk from the strategy's technical stop, divide to get share size (source 0).

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Accept the pre-planned stop without negotiation; exit as soon as the setup is invalidated.
Never average down a losing day trade.
Hitting the personal daily max-loss ends the trading day — treated as a hard circuit breaker.
Trade only recognized setups on in-play stocks; sitting out is a position.
Daily recap and journaling of trades is built into the routine he teaches.

extraction.agent_notes: Performance claims array left empty deliberately: no personal P&L is disclosed anywhere checkable. Excluded: (a) SSRN backtest returns (e.g., ORB study figures) — strategy simulations, not his record; (b) marketing-adjacent claims like students earning '1% a day' cited by critics — unverifiable. Reviews (source 4) report his birth name as Amin Aziznia while Wikipedia presents 'Andrew Aziz'; recorded as alias with attribution, not adjudicated. Wikipedia gives born 1983 -> born_era 1980s. Risk figures are prescriptive rules from his books — he presents them as his own practice, but there is no way to verify adherence.

entry.trigger_summary: Opening-only limit orders placed pre-open around projected opening prices on 10-300 symbols per trader, designed to get filled only on stocks that gap sharply up or down at the auction (roughly 5-20% of orders fill); pairs variant: on an extreme open in one stock, take the fill and hedge with a correlated peer (e.g., long the gapped-down name, short its sector twin). Also trades the close using MOC imbalance publications at 3:40 pm ET (sources 0, 3).
entry.notes: 'Other' archetype = opening-auction envelope orders (a mechanism, not a chart pattern). Strategy is capital-intensive: he stated it takes a couple million dollars of buying power (source 0).

exit.notes: Disclosed personal routine: immediately covers half the filled shares (typically 2,000-4,000 per stock) at about 6-10 cents profit, then works out of the rest based on market movement, peers, and sector behavior; some firm traders automate retrace orders and stop-loss orders for non-retracing fills (source 0). Stop placement basis not stated.

risk.notes: No numeric personal risk parameters disclosed; risk control is structural (limit-price envelopes, immediate partial profit, stop-loss orders on the remainder, pair hedges).

sizing.notes: Order sizes of 2,000-4,000 shares per symbol mentioned descriptively (source 0); no sizing formula disclosed.

claims.note: His own statement that the opening-only strategy was historically profitable about 75% of the time or more; strategy-level, self-reported, unaudited.

entry.trigger_summary: The mechanical system he and William Eckhardt taught the Turtles entered on Donchian channel breakouts: System 1 on 20-day highs/lows, System 2 on 55-day highs/lows. His own earlier pit trading was more discretionary but followed the same trend-with-breakout logic (hence discretion = hybrid).
entry.notes: System 1 also had a rule outside this taxonomy: skip the 20-day breakout if the previous breakout signal would have been a winner (take the 55-day failsafe instead). Position limits capped units in closely correlated markets.

exit.notes: Initial stop at 2N (twice the 20-day ATR-like N) from entry; the effective trailing exit was an opposite Donchian breakout (10-day for System 1, 20-day for System 2), exiting the entire position at once.

risk_per_trade_pct.note: Derivation: the published rules size one unit so that a 1N price move equals about 1% of account equity, and the initial stop is 2N from entry, so one unit risks about 2% of equity. Arithmetic combination of two stated rules; applies to the taught Turtle system, not a disclosed personal number for Dennis's own pit trading.

max_drawdown_rule.note: Turtle rules: for each 10% drawdown, trade as if the account were 20% smaller, restoring size as equity recovers.

portfolio_heat_cap.note: Turtle position limits: max 4 units per market, 6 units in closely correlated markets, 12 units total in one direction. Pyramiding added units at 0.5N intervals up to the 4-unit market cap.

risk.notes: All numeric risk rules here are from the published system he taught the Turtles; Dennis never publicly disclosed equivalent parameters for his own earlier discretionary trading.

sizing.notes: N-based (ATR-style) unit sizing so each unit represented roughly equal volatility exposure across markets (Original Turtle Rules).

psychology_rules.paraphrase: The system's profitability depended on staying with the few large trends; the many small breakout losses were paid for by rare big winners.
Believed good trading was reducible to teachable rules consistently applied - the premise of the Turtle experiment, run to settle his nature-vs-nurture debate with Eckhardt.
Losses were capped mechanically at the 2N stop with no discretion to hold beyond it.

claims.note: Reported fortune built from a small borrowed stake (about $1,600 borrowed, most spent on a MidAm exchange seat, leaving roughly $400 of trading capital). Widely reported; never published as an audited record.

entry.trigger_summary: Specializes in recent IPOs and super-growth stocks: classifies each stock into one of six empirically derived lifecycle patterns (late bloomers, pump-and-dumps, stair steppers, rocket ships, one-hit wonders, disappointments) and commits to a sell rule in advance matched to the stock's lifecycle phase; entries come from post-IPO bases/breakouts within that framework.
entry.notes: Discretion coded 'hybrid' because the framework prescribes explicit, pre-chosen phase-based sell rules derived from proprietary historical IPO research while stock selection remains judgment-based. psychology_rules.paraphrase: The authors stress that patience is essential with IPOs - most need time and repeated bases before their durable advance, so the framework discourages chasing the first move.
Preserve 'mental capital' alongside financial capital: MCP stops exist to exit positions before open losses or round-tripped gains impair the trader's judgment for future decisions.

entry.trigger_summary: Speculate only in active, liquid, leading stocks of leading groups, bought when already moving and demonstrating strength, with the aim of capturing a substantial gain rather than small profits; commit meaningfully only when evidence and conviction are strongly aligned, otherwise stay largely in cash reserves. (Paraphrased from The Battle for Investment Survival.)
entry.notes: Loeb stressed marketability — big, actively traded issues one can exit instantly — and earnings/quality awareness alongside price leadership. He rejected wide diversification as, in paraphrase, an admission of ignorance: concentrate in a few well-watched positions instead.

exit.notes: Sell promptly when a position shows roughly a 10% loss (see risk); on the profit side he argued small gains are not worth the risk taken — aim for large moves and sell when the reason for holding no longer exists. Mechanical trailing/scale-out procedures not documented.

risk_per_trade_pct.note: Loeb's loss-acceptance rule: close a position losing about 10% from cost. Corroborated by O'Neil (source 1) crediting Loeb with the 10% cut-loss rule. Price-based stop distance, not percent of equity risked.

risk.notes: He advocated holding substantial cash reserves and committing only a portion of capital to speculation at any time, but stated no fixed percentage — undisclosed.

sizing.notes: Concentration in a few positions sized by strength of conviction/evidence, with the rest in cash reserve; explicitly anti-diversification for the speculator. No numeric formula given.

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Accepting losses quickly is the single most important device for protecting capital; the loss taken is insurance against ruin.
Stay in cash until an opportunity is compelling; being fully invested at all times is a losing habit for the speculator.
Small profits do not pay for the risks of speculation — seek positions capable of substantial gains and give them room to develop.

extraction.agent_notes: No quantitative performance claims retained: the oft-repeated story that Loeb largely sidestepped the 1929 crash carries no number and no primary source, so it is recorded only as a caution-flag-level anecdote. His wealth figures found online are aggregator-only and excluded. The durable content is his rule set: 10% loss cutting, concentration over diversification, liquidity of leading issues, large cash reserves. Note his book frames everything as 'speculation' consciously — closer to modern momentum trading than investing.

entry.trigger_summary: Waits for price to break decisively through a 'pivotal point' — a prior resistance/support level or psychologically important price — after consolidation, then enters in the direction of the break. Commits capital in installments: an initial probe, adding only if the market moves in his favor and confirms the judgment. Watches volume and price behavior at the pivot for confirmation. (Paraphrased from How to Trade in Stocks, 1940.)
entry.notes: Filters paraphrased: he first judged the general market's direction ('line of least resistance') and only traded stocks in harmony with it, concentrating on the leading stocks of leading industry groups (his prescreened, actively followed list). 'market_health_index' used loosely for his overall-market check — no formal index existed.

exit.notes: Stop was typically a mental rule (max ~10% adverse move on committed capital, rooted in bucket-shop margin) rather than a resting order. Exits on winners were discretionary/tape-based: abnormal market behavior after an extended move, failure at pivotal points. Whether he trailed stops mechanically or scaled out systematically is not documented — left null.

risk_per_trade_pct.note: His stated rule: never sustain a loss of more than 10% of the capital committed to a trade. This is a price-based tolerance on the position, NOT percent of total equity risked.

risk.notes: Pyramiding documented in How to Trade in Stocks (staged buying as price confirms). Smitten reports he periodically moved profits into cash/annuities after big wins, yet he still went bankrupt repeatedly — rule adherence was inconsistent (see caution_flags).

sizing.notes: How to Trade in Stocks describes committing a line of stock in installments (e.g., an initial ~20% probe, completing the position only as price action confirms). Habitually used heavy broker margin; no consistent leverage figure disclosed.

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Take a small loss immediately when a trade shows it is wrong; hoping and holding turns small losses into ruinous ones.
Never add to a losing position to lower the average price — additional purchases belong only to positions proving themselves profitable.
The big money comes from sitting through the major move once right, not from trading in and out around it.
Stay out of the market entirely until a pivotal point sets up; there are times when the correct position is cash and inactivity.

claims.note: Profit from shorting into the 1929 crash, widely reported by contemporary press and repeated by biographers. Pre-SEC era — never audited; treat as reported, not verified.
Reported single-day short-side profit during the October 1907 panic; source is the semi-fictionalized Reminiscences account.

entry.trigger_summary: Three self-described core setups: (1) continuation breakout — a stock that has already made a strong momentum move consolidates in a tightening flag/range, entered as it clears the range high; (2) episodic pivot — a large gap on a surprise catalyst (often earnings), entered intraday as it lifts from the opening range; (3) parabolic short — fading an unsustainable vertical extension ('other' archetype).
entry.notes: Candidates come from daily momentum and episodic-pivot scans of the strongest-moving, sufficiently liquid names (sources 0, 2). Parabolic short mapped to 'other' — no vocabulary value for parabolic-reversal shorts.

exit.notes: Sells a portion (described variously as ~20-25% or 1/3-1/2) into strength after the first 3-5 days of the move, moves the stop on the remainder to breakeven, then trails with the 10- or 20-day moving average depending on the stock's speed; initial stop typically at the low of the entry day (source 1). He has said traders "can't outsmart the 10- and 20-day moving averages" (source 1).

risk_per_trade_pct.note: States usual risk of 0.25-1% of the account per trade at current size, rarely above 1%; said he risked roughly 0.5-1.5% when the account was smaller. Recorded as the stated 1% ceiling.

risk.notes: Moves stop to breakeven after the initial partial sale into strength (source 1). Aggregator claims of 10-25% position sizes were excluded (no primary source located).

sizing.notes: Position size derived from the fixed percentage-of-equity risk and the stop distance (source 1).

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Keeps individual trade risk to a small fraction of equity and exits immediately at the day-low stop when a breakout fails.
After banking a partial into strength, refuses to guess at tops — holds the rest until the 10- or 20-day moving average is lost.
Runs daily scans and waits for the small number of qualifying setups in leading stocks rather than trading everything that moves.

entry.trigger_summary: Enters on completion breakouts of classical horizontal chart patterns (rectangles, right-angle triangles, head-and-shoulders) that offer an asymmetric reward-to-risk profile; each Friday he selects roughly ten candidate markets for the coming week and restricts trading to them; orders are entered once a day (late afternoon, tweaked pre-open) rather than watching intraday ticks.
entry.notes: Self-described swing trader, not an investor: a four-month-old trade 'has gray hair' by his standard. Trades roughly 100 times a year (down from 30-35/month in the early 1980s). Favors patterns where entrenched conventional wisdom looks wrong on the chart. All from source 0.

exit.notes: Initial risk of 80-100 bps is squeezed down as fast as the market allows - target is ~30 bps or breakeven within two to three days of entry; trades that challenge him within two to three days are cut (part of a trade is timing, not just direction). Has explicit rules for layering out of winners as well as layering in. Classical-charting measured targets per source 2. Sources 0 and 2.

risk_per_trade_pct.note: Stated as a max of 80-100 basis points of total nominal assets per trade; corroborated by his own Factor Q&A (source 3). Risk is reduced quickly after entry toward ~30 bps or breakeven.

Describes himself as a risk manager first, trade identification as the least important of four ingredients of trading.

sizing.notes: Position size derived from the fixed basis-point risk budget divided by entry-to-stop distance; puts on larger size in low-volatility markets (e.g., Turkish lira 2018, yuan 2015-16) because the same bp budget allows it (source 0).

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Cutting losses short is the exchange-floor adage he says successful proprietary traders actually live by, not just recite; his default expectation entering any trade is that it will lose money, which enforces extra risk diligence.

Once a trade is comfortably profitable he resists taking quick profits on the whole position and lets it run, guarding against his own impatience, which he identifies as the trait that would cut his winners short.

Distinguishes mistakes (process errors) from losing trades: a stupid trade can profit and a well-executed plan can lose. He channels an obsessive personality into obsession with process, order flow, and knowing his own trading metrics.
Submits his performance annually to a formal advisory board of traders who challenge whether he traded the way he said he would and interrogate his risk management.

However convinced he is about a market's direction, he operates on the premise that he doesn't actually know and may well be wrong; charts describe trend, congestion, and asymmetric opportunities - they do not predict price.

entry.trigger_summary: Enter long after an accumulation trading range matures: a successful spring or secondary test on shrinking volume, followed by a sign of strength — a rally through range resistance on widening price spread and expanding volume — with entry preferred on the subsequent pullback (last point of support). A checklist of buying tests (trend of market, behavior vs the market, preparation/cause built, supply exhausted) must be satisfied. Reverse logic for shorts in distribution. (Paraphrased from the 1931 course.)
entry.notes: Method starts from the general market's position and trend ('market_health_index' used loosely — his composite-index judgment), then selects the stocks strongest/weakest relative to the market from the followed list. Core doctrine: infer the intentions of large 'composite operator' interests from price, volume, and spread alone.

exit.notes: Stop orders placed just beyond the structural point that invalidates the trade (below support/spring low for longs); course instructs raising stops progressively as the move advances. Price objectives projected from point-and-figure horizontal counts of the accumulation 'cause'; exits also taken on behavior signaling the move's end (shortening thrust, climactic volume).

risk.notes: The course mandates stop placement and risk-vs-reward comparison before entry (favorable ratio of projected objective to stop distance) but discloses no percent-of-equity figures — undisclosed.

sizing.notes: No numeric sizing formula in the published method; era practice was heavy margin but his personal usage is not reliably documented.

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Judge the market solely by its own action — price, volume, and their relationship — not by news, tips, or opinions.
Wait for the preparation (accumulation or distribution) to complete and for the tests to pass; trades taken before the cause is built are gambling.
Every commitment carries a stop order placed where the trade's reasoning is proven wrong, and it is honored without negotiation.

entry.trigger_summary: Buy when a stock breaks out above the resistance top of a Stage 1 base into Stage 2, on volume expanding to roughly double recent norms, with the 30-week moving average no longer declining and price above it, and Mansfield relative strength versus the market improving/turning positive. entry.notes: Forest-to-trees discipline (paraphrased): check overall market stage and breadth first, then the industry group's stage, and only then buy individual stocks — never buy a stock below a declining 30-week MA regardless of story.

exit.notes: Initial protective sell-stop goes under the breakout point/nearest support at time of purchase; stops are then ratcheted up under successive swing lows and the 30-week MA as Stage 2 progresses. risk.notes: The book prescribes WHERE stops go (structure) but no percent-of-equity risk figure, drawdown rule, or heat cap — undisclosed, not zero.

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Never buy without simultaneously entering a protective sell-stop, and never cancel or lower it to stay in a losing trade.
Stay with a Stage 2 uptrend and trail the stop rather than grabbing quick profits; the method's edge is riding the full stage.
Never average down into a Stage 4 decline — cheapness is not a reason to buy a downtrending stock.
Do not anticipate bottoms or tops; act only after the chart demonstrates a stage transition.

entry.trigger_summary: Fixed-income convergence/relative-value: enter when spreads between economically linked instruments (on-the-run vs off-the-run Treasuries, swap spreads, European convergence trades) widen beyond model fair value, expecting mean reversion; later expanded into merger arbitrage and short equity volatility as core spreads shrank (Lowenstein).

exit.notes: Negative evidence, well documented: LTCM had no stop-loss regime — as spreads widened against it in 1998 the firm maintained and in places added to losing convergence positions on the conviction that spreads must revert, while its shrinking equity mechanically raised leverage (Lowenstein; PWG report). risk.notes: Risk was managed via VaR and correlation models calibrated to recent history; the 1998 episode showed the assumptions (stable correlations, available liquidity) failed jointly. sizing.notes: Positions sized at portfolio level from model-estimated expected return and VaR contribution, then levered aggressively because individual spread trades carried tiny margins.

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Cautionary case: institutional conviction that mean reversion was near-certain led to doubling down and refusing to cut losers; the missing rule (cut losses / cap exposure) is the documented lesson rather than a rule he followed.

sizing.notes: Post-LTCM published framework (biased-coin paper; The Missing Billionaires): size positions by expected utility, in practice a fraction of full Kelly (he suggests around a third to a half) because edge and variance estimates are uncertain. psychology_rules.paraphrase: How much you bet matters as much as what you bet on — sizing, not selection, is the decision that ruins otherwise-skilled investors.

Cautionary lesson he draws from LTCM: maintaining or growing outsized positions as losses mount converts a bad year into ruin; exposure should shrink as capital and edge confidence shrink.

psychology_rules.paraphrase: Argues an average system followed with total discipline beats a superior system applied inconsistently; overriding the models to reduce risk rarely worked out over the long run.

Keeps a hard stop on every trade to preserve capital, prioritizing staying in the game over volatility optimization.

entry.trigger_summary: Researcher-practitioner rather than discretionary trader: as chief research strategist and co-portfolio manager of AlphaSimplex's managed-futures strategy, she runs systematic time-series-momentum models — long assets with positive recent trends, short those with negative trends — across liquid global equity, bond, currency and commodity futures/forwards, typically blending multiple signal speeds. Her book formalizes this as rules-based divergent trend following whose payoff ('crisis alpha') concentrates in extended market dislocations.
entry.notes: Specific production-signal parameters of the AlphaSimplex program are proprietary; the description paraphrases the fund's stated pure trend-following mandate (source 3) and her published research framework (sources 1, 5).

exit.notes: In the representative trend systems of her published research, positions are reduced or reversed when the trend signal flips; production-fund stop mechanics are not disclosed, so initial_stop_basis stays undisclosed (sources 1, 3).

risk.notes: Her research and the fund's materials emphasize volatility-based risk allocation and portfolio-level risk management, but no personal numeric risk rules are disclosed — nulls throughout.

sizing.notes: Per her published work: trend-following positions are sized inversely to estimated volatility (equal-risk allocation across markets), with portfolio-construction/optimization overlays — a research-documented model attribution (sources 1, 5), not a disclosed production parameter set.

psychology_rules.paraphrase: "When you're a systematic investor, your process makes the decision" — her stated view that discipline lives in the researched process, with the human role being to design and maintain it, not to override trades.
Her crisis-alpha framework argues trend following profits by reacting to price dislocations as they unfold rather than by predicting crises in advance.

entry.trigger_summary: As taught in the Turtle program: enter long/short on a one-tick break of the prior 20-day high/low (System 1 — skipped if the previous S1 breakout in that market was a winner, with a 55-day failsafe breakout so major moves are never missed) or of the prior 55-day high/low (System 2).
entry.notes: Method documented here is the 1984-88 taught system (source 3), the period covered by her verified 114.1%-a-year record. EMC's later production systems were proprietary — Cheval described an ongoing research process to adapt strategies to future market conditions (source 2) — so firm-era entry specifics, timeframe and holding period are not publicly specified; 'daily' bars and 'weeks' holding reflect the documented taught system. Unit position limits across correlated markets acted as an entry gate (see risk).

exit.notes: Taught system: initial stop 2N (N = 20-day EMA of true range); winners exited on a 10-day (S1) or 20-day (S2) breakout against the position — a trailing channel exit, never a profit target; all units in a position exited together (source 3).

risk_per_trade_pct.note: Derivation: rules size 1 unit so a 1N price move ≈ 1% of account equity, and the initial stop is 2N ⇒ ≈2% of equity at risk per unit (½N 'whipsaw' stop variant risked ½% per unit). Up to 4 units per market via pyramiding.

max_drawdown_rule.note: Turtles cut the notional account 20% each time it fell 10% from the original size, compounding the cut on further 10% losses.

portfolio_heat_cap.note: Unit limits: 4 per market, 6 in closely correlated markets, 10 in loosely correlated markets, 12 total in a single direction (1 unit ≈ 1% equity volatility per N).

risk.notes: All figures describe the taught 1984-88 Turtle system (source 3). Units added at ½N intervals with stops on earlier units raised ½N per add (not a strict move-to-breakeven, hence null). EMC-era risk parameters undisclosed.

sizing.notes: N-based (ATR) unit sizing normalized risk per market so more-volatile markets got fewer contracts per unit (source 3).

psychology_rules.paraphrase: A lasting operation needs two things: a strategy that works now and a reliable research method for adapting it to future market conditions.
She emphasized disciplined execution of both the trading rules and the research process, treating the P&L record as the only arbiter.

entry.trigger_summary: Two published mechanical systems. (1) The weekly/4-week rule (the original Donchian channel): buy and cover shorts when price exceeds the highs of the prior four full calendar weeks; sell and go short on a new 4-week low — an always-in-the-market reversal system. (2) The 5- and 20-day moving average method (developed at Hayden Stone, 1960): trade in the direction of a 20-day MA crossing, but only after price penetrates the MA by a preset number of price-scaled units (e.g., larger absolute penetration required for higher-priced commodities) with day-sequencing confirmation rules; the 5-day MA governs shorter-term liquidation.
entry.notes: His general guides tell traders to treat volume expansion after a quiet period as significant, and his supplemental 5/20 rules require minimum penetration before acting — paraphrased from sources 2-3. The 4-week rule itself has no confirmation conditions.

exit.notes: In the 4-week system the exit is the opposite channel signal (position reverses at a new 4-week extreme against you). In the 5/20 method, longs are liquidated when price closes back below the 5-day MA (with confirmation), shorts vice versa. His guidelines separately advise 'judicious' use of stop orders placed with reference to chart formations to cap losses and protect profits — hence structure/chart-based initial stop basis (sources 2-3).

risk.notes: He published qualitative risk guidance (limit losses, protect profits with stops, trade light when direction is unclear) but no numeric per-trade risk, drawdown or heat rules — all fields honestly null (source 2).

sizing.notes: Mapped from his published general guides: carry light commitments when market direction is uncertain and heavier positions when a sustained move is anticipated (he also noted long-side advances tend to yield larger percentage gains than equal declines). Qualitative rule, no numbers (source 2).

psychology_rules.paraphrase: His overriding published guideline — "limit losses and ride profits, irrespective of all other rules" (Donchian, trading guidelines) — put loss-cutting above every other consideration.
The companion half of the same overriding guide: stay with a clearly defined sustained move and let the trend produce the profit rather than taking it early.
Act only on clearly defined moves and stand aside in sideways ranges; he warned that trading indistinct conditions produces whipsaw losses, and against hasty decisions driven by popular opinion.
